transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Redwood CSM); Liam Chen (Valence CTO), Marta Alvarez (ML Eng), Noah Rivers (SRE), Tara Singh (Product)

[00:00] Jordan Blake: hey everyone thanks for joining, should we do quick intros?
[00:08] Liam Chen: yeah hi I'm Liam CTO at Valence, we run customer-facing LLM endpoints for search and summarization, keen to understand how hard a swap would be.
[00:15] Marta Alvarez: Marta here, I own the inference pipelines and the prompts, mainly worried about tokenization and changing output distribution.
[00:22] Priya Nair: cool thanks, i'll run through parity mapping and then show console and optimize suggestions. we built some helpers for teams moving off OpenAI/Anthropic/Together so you'll see concrete examples.
[00:35] Jordan Blake: objective for today: map your current endpoints to Redwood equivalents, surface risks (latency/cost/qa), and agree next steps for a short pilot.
[00:44] Tara Singh: timeline wise product needs a pilot in staging in the next two weeks ideally.
[00:48] Jordan Blake: we'll try to hit that.
[00:52] [01:05] Priya Nair: first topic: tokenization and prompt mapping. OpenAI and Together use similar BPE tokenizers but there are edge-case differences for emojis and non-ascii. in our mapping script we include a tokenizer sanity check — counts both model-based and generic utf-8 heuristics. this helps predict cost deltas.
[01:30] Marta Alvarez: can we see an example where it changes behavior? we had a case where summaries got truncated when we moved model versions.
[01:35] Priya Nair: yeah, show slide 3 — if you have aggressive stop sequences or system role injections the token boundaries can shift which affects streaming chunk sizes.
[01:42] [01:50] Priya Nair: (screen) here is a small snippet: original request to OpenAI with "system: you are a summarizer", and same prompt to Redwood — we recommend explicit stop tokens and an explicit max_tokens calculated post-tokenize. also call out any model-specific special tokens.
[02:10] Noah Rivers: our SRE cares about latency tail — 95th percentile spikes during peak. how does Redwood's batching and KV caching affect that?
[02:18] Priya Nair: good question — Redwood runtime supports continuous batching but you can tune per-route SLOs. for critical low-latency routes we suggest smaller batch windows and enable prefix KV caching for repeated context (like user history). that reduces compute per token.
[02:33] Jordan Blake: and if you need consistency, dedicated pools give SLA backed latency and capacity.
[02:40] Liam Chen: dedicated is attractive but procurement will push back on cost. what's the typical cost delta?
[02:46] Priya Nair: depends on throughput pattern; our Optimize tool will produce a cost vs latency curve from your traffic profile. we often find a mixed approach: hosted for infrequent flows, dedicated for hot endpoints.
[02:58] [03:05] Marta Alvarez: function calling — we use structured responses a lot. Together's model has specific behavior when returning JSON, sometimes trailing commas. how compatible is Redwood's function-calling shim?
[03:14] Priya Nair: Redwood supports function/tool calls and structured output. we implemented tolerant JSON parsing and optional schema validation step in the Console/Optimize pipeline. the parity mapping includes heuristics to convert Together-style outputs into our standard tool-calling format.
[03:30] Tara Singh: are there differences in streaming? we rely on tokens arriving asap for UI snappiness.
[03:34] Priya Nair: streaming works similarly — Redwood streams chunked deltas. nuance: some models stream per-token vs per-chunk; our SDK exposes backpressure and a streaming buffer size param. if you had a Together integration that expected per-token events, we can emulate that in the adapter.
[03:52] [04:05] Jordan Blake: security/compliance — high level: Redwood offers Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem) with KMS integrations. Ethan, you want add the security bit?
[04:13] Ethan Cole: sure — we will attach SOC2 Type II report, evidence of KMS/HSM integrations, SSO/SAML support and audit logs. dedicated and private include network isolation; private can be air-gapped for regulated workloads.
[04:25] Liam Chen: we need KMS that integrates with AWS KMS and GCP KMS plus audit trails per request. is that supported?
[04:31] Ethan Cole: yes we support external KMS and detailed per-request telemetry in the Console. we'll drop the security pack into CRM after this meeting.
[04:40] [04:50] Marta Alvarez: on the data plane: can we keep embeddings on-prem for PII workloads?
[04:54] Priya Nair: Private deployment supports customer-managed data plane; embeddings can be kept in your VPC with customer-managed storage. we also support token redaction and retention policies in Console.
[05:05] Noah Rivers: network peering — what's required for VPC peering?
[05:09] Jordan Blake: typically a single peering with egress restrictions and a small set of allowed IPs. we'll provide a checklist.
[05:16] [05:20] Priya Nair: demo time — quick walkthrough of Console. (screen) here you can create a route, pin a model version, and set rollout policy. note the per-route batching controls and a toggle for prefix KV caching.
[05:36] Priya Nair: (click) here's Optimize: it suggests quantization profile and batching params for your workload. you can simulate cost impact by uploading a sample traffic file — that will be part of the pilot.
[05:48] [06:00] Priya Nair: also showing the parity mapping snippet in repo — it contains mappings for system prompts, function-call marshalling, and tokenization checks. we'll share this after the call.
[06:10] Marta Alvarez: cool, will that handle role-based system messages? we pass role: assistant/system sometimes differently across vendors.
[06:16] Priya Nair: yes, there's a normalization layer that maps vendor role names and merges system messages; it's configurable.
[06:23] [06:30] Liam Chen: how do we validate output quality? we need A/B tests and regression alerts.
[06:35] Priya Nair: Redwood has eval hooks — you can attach prompt suites with expected outputs; the Console runs periodic regression checks and triggers alerts. Optimize can prioritize models by quality vs cost.
[06:47] [06:55] Tara Singh: ok final ask: what would a minimal pilot look like?
[06:58] Jordan Blake: two endpoints in staging — a low-latency chat route and a higher-throughput embedding route. benchmark for 72 hours, run quality evals and cost sims.
[07:10] Priya Nair: we'll provide the mapping script, SDK examples in node/python, and a prebuilt traffic file template.
[07:18] Ethan Cole: and i'll attach security docs.
[07:22] [07:30] Liam Chen: sounds good. one more: are there runtime differences that could change hallucination rates?
[07:34] Priya Nair: hallucinations are usually model-behavior driven; Redwood can't change base model semantics but can help with prompt templates, instruction enforcement, and reranking. Optimize suggests candidate model variants and reranking thresholds.
[07:50] Marta Alvarez: ok thanks, that clarifies a lot.
[07:55] Jordan Blake: quick recap and next steps — Priya shares parity mapping script and SDK examples; Ethan uploads security pack; Valence sends prompt set and traffic profile; Jordan schedules pilot kickoff.
[08:10] Liam Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up once we gather logs.
[08:15] Jordan Blake: thanks everyone, end.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts present — some model and product names transcribed inconsistently. Links referenced during demo: https://redwood.example.com/parity-mapping (shared), console screenshot, and a sample traffic CSV (to be shared).
